1. A syllable with a doubled vowel (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) always takes the stress. No word has more than one.
2. Otherwise, if the word ends in a consonant, stress the last syllable.
3. Otherwise, if the second-to-last syllable ends in a consonant, stress the second-to-last syllable.
4. Otherwise, stress the third-to-last syllable.

questions.stem:
Words: bird = birdo, woman = woma, house = housa, boy = boyi, happy = hap-, big = big-, old = old-, three = thri.
Which phrase follows every rule?
questions.passage:
Rules for this section:
1. An adjective comes after the noun it describes.
2. An adjective is a stem ending in a consonant (blak- = black). It takes the last vowel of its noun's root: dogo (dog) gives dogo blako.
3. Plural: add -s to the noun and to each of its adjectives.
4. After a number word (tuo = two, thri = three, fora = four), the number comes first and neither the noun nor its adjectives take -s.
5. With two adjectives, both follow the noun in the REVERSE of the English order.
6. There is no word for "the" or "a".
questions.explanation: thri birdo bigo hapo ("three happy big birds") follows every rule: bird = birdo; three = thri first, no -s; happy and big take o from birdo, order reversed. woma hapa thri puts the number word after the noun instead of first (correct: thri woma hapa). thri biga housa puts the adjective before the noun, but adjectives always follow it (correct: thri housa biga). boyi bigis oldis puts -s on the adjective but not on the noun (correct: boyis bigis oldis).
